title: Picking Exactly
subtitle: An exact sign cascade for argmax on 32-bit floats, its cost, and what training it really shows.

chapters.title: The Sign Cascade
chapters.blurb: Relu of a gap, scaled by two to the twenty-third and clamped, seven times, turns the smallest float difference into exactly one.
captions: Picking the biggest of several scores sounds easy. Inside a handwired circuit it has to be exact, even when two scores differ only in their very last bit.
The circuit has only weighted sums, relu, and products gated by a relu. Relu keeps a positive number as it is and turns a negative one into zero.
We want one bit from two scores: one if the right score is strictly larger, zero otherwise. A tie must give zero, so the left candidate wins.
Step one is relu of the right score minus the left. That is zero for a tie or a left win, and positive for a right win, but possibly absurdly small.
How small? The smallest positive gap between thirty-two-bit floats is two to the minus one hundred forty-nine. Nothing downstream would call that a one.
So the circuit multiplies by two to the twenty-third. Multiplying by a power of two only shifts the exponent, so the gap grows without losing any precision.
Then a clamp caps the value at one. The clamp is the value minus relu of the value minus one, and it stays exact for anything below two to the twenty-fourth.
Each multiply and each clamp is marked as its own rounding point, one the simplifier may not merge away. Otherwise the stages would collapse into one formula.
Seven multiplies by two to the twenty-third give a total gain of two to the hundred sixty-one. Watch the smallest gap climb through the stages.
After the first multiply it is two to the minus one hundred twenty-six. After the seventh it is two to the twelfth, and the final clamp pins it at exactly one.
A bigger gap saturates earlier and stays at one. A tie is zero, and zero times anything is still zero, so the left candidate keeps its win.
The result is a bit made only of sums, relu, and scaling. The lab's report counts zero boolean atoms in it.

chapters.title: Eight Candidates, One Winner
chapters.blurb: A tournament of those bits picks one winner, beating the production argmax on near-ties at about three and a half times the built operations.
captions: One bit compares two candidates. Eight candidates need a tournament: pair them up, compare each pair, and send the winners on to the next round.
Each match makes a right-wins bit and a left-wins bit, which is one minus it. The winner's score rises through two gated products, and the route is kept as a one-hot.
Both argmax versions aim at the same rule: the leftmost maximum wins. The lab's test oracle is simply that rule written in plain code.
The production argmax scales the gap to near one half and rounds it with a boolean atom. A tie goes left there too.
But that encoding also keeps the left candidate across a rounding band. The lab's header puts it at roughly two point four in ten million, and its test bounds it under two point five.
Plant one candidate a single float step above the leader. In the lab's test the cascade picks it, at position six, while production keeps position two.
The tests cover ties at many magnitudes, tiny subnormal gaps, adjacent floats, and two thousand random vectors at each of four widths. Both evaluators agree.
Say it plainly: that is sampled testing, not a proof for every pair of scores. It also assumes scores stay between zero and one.
Now the price. At eight candidates, production builds fifty-six operations in fifteen layers. The cascade builds one hundred ninety-six in seventy-five.
At sixty-four candidates it is five hundred four against one thousand seven hundred sixty-four operations, and thirty-three layers against one hundred fifty.
Those are built operations, counted before compiling. Compiled, the cascade is still about four times larger: forty-five against one hundred eighty-seven at eight candidates.
The lab calls the cascade an available construction, not a proof of minimality. The core's own exact tree is one hundred fifty operations in fifty-seven layers, counted after compiling.

chapters.title: Training It Soft
chapters.blurb: Soft ramps, annealed gains and hardening fit a 128-cell table to 160 of 160 winners, and the lab says what that does not show.
captions: Writing a circuit by hand is one thing. Can its scores be learned? The hard cascade is exact, but a hard decision hands back no useful gradient.
The lab measured it. For separated scores, a tie, and the smallest possible gap, the gradient reaching the scores was exactly zero.
So training uses the same topology, soft. The seven scale factors shrink from two to the twenty-third to a gentle gain, and each clamp turns into a ramp.
The ramp is centered on a zero gap, so a tie sits mid-ramp and a wrong decision gets gradient from both orderings.
The task is small. Sixteen cases, eight candidates, and one learned score for every case and candidate: a table of one hundred twenty-eight cells.
Training anneals the total gain in five steps, from eight up to about two million, with up to one hundred fifty epochs at each, stopping early once every case is right.
The weights start close together near one half, so every comparison sits inside the widest ramp and receives gradient from the first epoch.
Then comes hardening. The same weights go into the exact cascade, and every winner must come out exact in both evaluators.
Across ten seeds, all one hundred sixty winners came out right after hardening. That result holds for this table and these seeds.
A control with a single clipped ramp, with under half the operations, also reaches one hundred sixty of one hundred sixty on ten fresh seeds.
So this is per-case table fitting. There is no shared query and key rule, and no claim about contexts the table never saw.
The scorecard: the exact forward construction holds, the learning claim is narrow, and useful gradients through the hard cascade are still missing.
